nodes.label: Indoor air quality

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_000
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is a potential consequence of implementing tighter building envelopes and improved insulation?
nodes.answer: They can inadvertently increase indoor radon concentrations by reducing natural ventilation.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_001
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What factors affect indoor radon concentration (IRC) according to the article?
nodes.answer: Indoor radon concentration is affected by geological properties of the site, architectural features of the building, occupants' habits, and prevailing meteorological conditions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_002
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What role do occupant ventilation habits play regarding indoor radon levels?
nodes.answer: Occupant ventilation habits play a significant role in indoor radon levels, as the relationship between seasons and radon concentrations can vary globally depending on these habits.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_003
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why is it important to improve indoor comfort in traditional houses on the Sichuan Plateau?
nodes.answer: Improving indoor comfort is important to enhance the quality of life for residents, protect cultural heritage, and contribute to environmental protection and sustainable development.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How can storms and high winds influence radon movement within buildings?
nodes.answer: They can affect indoor air pressure, thereby influencing the movement of radon into and within buildings.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_005
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Which elements have previous studies mainly focused on regarding IRC?
nodes.answer: Previous studies have mainly examined the influence of meteorological factors on indoor radon concentration (IRC).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_006
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What does the data in Tables 1 and 2 demonstrate about indoor radon concentrations?
nodes.answer: The data demonstrates substantial geographical variation in indoor radon concentrations influenced by climatic, geological, and anthropogenic factors.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_007
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What aspects of indoor environment were residents asked about during the interviews?
nodes.answer: Residents responded to questions about indoor temperature, humidity, air quality, and symptoms such as feeling cold, hot, stuffy, or wet.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_008
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Which seasons are typically associated with higher indoor radon concentrations?
nodes.answer: Research indicates that cool seasons are often associated with elevated indoor radon concentrations compared to warm periods.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_009
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What aspects of the indoor environment were evaluated in the questionnaire survey?
nodes.answer: The survey evaluated indoor temperature, humidity, air quality, and residents' feelings about cold, heat, stuffiness, and wetness.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_010
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How did the indoor temperature and relative humidity compare to local standards during the study?
nodes.answer: The indoor temperature range was 13.3 to 22.3 °C, and the relative humidity range was 69.1 to 83.0%, indicating that the thermal environment did not meet local standards due to high humidity.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_011
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: How did the indoor temperature and humidity compare to the local standards?
nodes.answer: The indoor temperature range was 13.3 to 32.3 °C, and the relative humidity was between 69.1 to 83.0%, which did not meet the requirements of the local standards.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_012
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What types of information were included in the interview content regarding residents' thermal comfort?
nodes.answer: The interview content included information on indoor temperature, humidity, air quality, and symptoms like feeling cold, hot, stuffy, or wet, as well as the use of temperature and humidity regulating equipment.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_013
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What new focus does this article introduce regarding indoor radon concentration?
nodes.answer: The article introduces a focus on the significant impact of geological factors, building characteristics, and occupants' behavior, in addition to meteorological conditions, on indoor radon concentration.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_014
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What were the weighted mean indoor radon concentration and its standard deviation found in the reviewed studies?
nodes.answer: The weighted mean indoor radon concentration was 178 Bq/m3, with a standard deviation of 193 Bq/m3.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_015
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What causes elevated indoor radon concentrations in homes during summer in Arizona and Alabama?
nodes.answer: Elevated indoor radon concentrations during summer in Arizona and Alabama are partly due to homes being tightly sealed and air-conditioned, which limits ventilation.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_016
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What factors can affect the efficacy of ventilation in reducing indoor radon concentrations?
nodes.answer: The efficacy of ventilation in reducing indoor radon concentrations can vary significantly based on specific construction practices and prevailing regional climate conditions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Good health and well-being|Environmental and occupational health|Indoor air quality_qna_017
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What impact do seasonal temperature variations have on indoor radon concentrations?
nodes.answer: Seasonal temperature variations significantly affect indoor radon concentrations; during colder months, homes are often sealed, leading to higher indoor radon levels, while warmer months may allow for enhanced ventilation that can lower these concentrations.
